name: Galleria Umberto I
label: Galleria Umberto I
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/242286729: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galleria Umberto I' (179 m across).

text.description:
Galleria Umberto I is a public shopping gallery in downtown Naples, directly across from the San Carlo opera house. It was built between 1887 and 1890 as part of the city's big rebuilding programme, the risanamento. The architect, Emanuele Rocco, drew on the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan. It is a tall, cross-shaped space with four glass-and-iron wings. A glass dome braced by 16 metal ribs rises above the crossing, 57 m high at the tip of its spire. Shops, cafés and flats were meant to share the building, and it is still a busy part of city life.

It photographs well because everything leads the eye upwards: curved ironwork, long arcades and a big patch of sky overhead. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the gallery's mapped outline. Walk to the crossing under the dome and look up for the most dramatic frame, then turn to face one of the arcades for a symmetrical view with people walking through. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and wipe your lens first, as pockets leave smears that show up against bright glass. If you want the outside too, the wing that opens towards the San Carlo theatre gives a different view from the one on via Toledo.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Naples, directly across from the San Carlo opera house. One wing of the gallery opens onto via Toledo (via Roma), the main downtown street.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Augusteo on the Centrale funicular, about 3 minutes on foot, with the Galleria to the east of the station. From Municipio (Metro Line 1 and Metro Line 6) it is about 5 minutes on foot, heading south-west. From the Via Colombo - Porto stop (tram 1 and tram 4) it is about 9 minutes on foot, heading west. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the dome and the full height of the arcades. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the long arcade views. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the ironwork and the glass roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then walk to the crossing under the dome if you want the dome overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: For the dome, hold the phone with the screen parallel to the wall and tilt up slowly, using the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For a symmetrical arcade, stand in the middle of a wing and line the centre gridline up with the middle of the roof. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or include a few people to show the scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a darker part of the gallery to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright glass roof doesn't wash out. Panorama mode works for a wing, but hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people. Daylight through the glass roof lights the gallery evenly, and the shops are likely to be lit in the evening.

text.access_note: This is a public shopping gallery that people walk through, but check the official site before you go for any access details.

Daylight through the glass roof lights the interior fairly evenly.

name: Spaccanapoli
label: Spaccanapoli
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo San Martino' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Largo San Martino' (way/506972915): point nearest the subject (182 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27179695: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Spaccanapoli is the long, straight street that cuts across the historic centre of Naples. It photographs well because it is so straight. From above, it reads as a single line drawn through a crowded patchwork of rooftops, with church domes and bell towers rising on either side. At street level the same straightness gives you a deep, narrow perspective, with buildings and laundry lines closing in on both sides.

For the classic overview, go to Largo San Martino, the open belvedere in front of the Certosa di San Martino in Vomero. Several guides call it the best view of the street's straight cut through the city. From here you look out over the rooftops towards the old town, and the street runs across the picture as a thin line. The view is high and fairly distant, so you will want your phone's telephoto lens.

If you would rather be in the thick of it, Via Benedetto Croce gives a straight-on view of the lane receding towards its eastern end. At the far end, Piazzetta Nilo frames the lane around the ancient statue of the Nile river-god. Allow time for both: the overview shows the scale, and the street-level views show the life of the place. Take care in narrow lanes with scooters and pedestrians, and stay out of the road when you line up a shot.
text.geographic_location: Spaccanapoli runs through the historic centre of Naples, east of Dante station and north of Università station. The overview point, Largo San Martino, is up the hill in Vomero, in front of the Certosa di San Martino.
text.directions_text: To see the street itself, take Metro Line 1 to Dante, about 6 minutes on foot from the street, or to Università, about 8 minutes on foot. For the overview, take one of the Vomero funiculars up to the Vomero district and walk to Largo San Martino, in front of the Certosa di San Martino. From the phone icon on the map, the street lies to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 1.1 km west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (3x-5x, depending on your phone) from Largo San Martino to pull the straight line of the street and the domes closer. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the street-level views.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.1 km west of the subject, in Largo San Martino (the phone icon on the map), and face east. At the belvedere in front of the Certosa di San Martino in Vomero. Look east across the rooftops of the historic centre to find the straight line of Spaccanapoli with the church domes and bell towers around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and let the straight line of the street run across the frame, with domes and bell towers as anchor points. Keep the rail or any foreground clutter out of the shot. As an alternative, Via Benedetto Croce gives a straight-on view of the lane receding eastwards. Piazzetta Nilo shows the far end around the Nile statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooftops to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky doesn't wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or brace it against a wall, to keep the zoomed shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day for the best light, and try morning to see what suits. The view is also clearer on a dry day with good visibility.

text.access_note: Largo San Martino is an open public square reached by the Vomero funiculars; check the funicular and any access closures before you go.

name: Piazza del Plebiscito
label: Piazza del Plebiscito
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (way/27182911): middle (276 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27182911: 'Statua equestre di Carlo di Borbone', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (277 m across).

text.description:
Piazza del Plebiscito is a very large, open square in central Naples, close to the Gulf of Naples. The Royal Palace closes it on the east side. On the west side is the church of San Francesco di Paola, with its curved twin colonnades reaching out to either side. The square is about 277 m across, so there is plenty of space to step back and fit things in. The statue of Charles of Bourbon on horseback stands in the middle of the paving.

It photographs well because nothing blocks the view. From the middle of the square you can look down Via Cesario Console, past the trees to the sea, with Vesuvius showing over the skyline. The colonnade and palace give strong, symmetrical lines for wider shots.

The square takes its name from the plebiscite of 21 October 1860, which brought Naples into the unified Kingdom of Italy. For a long time it was used as a car park. It was cleared and pedestrianised in 1994, when the G7 summit was held in Naples, which is why it feels so open today. The church's dome is 53 m high, so it stands out over the colonnades.

Go early, when it is quiet, and check for events first, as the square is sometimes used for concerts and can be crowded. If you want a second angle, try the curved colonnade from near the church, or the Royal Palace belvedere for a view over the whole square.
text.geographic_location: In central Naples, close to the waterfront on the Gulf of Naples. The square sits between the Royal Palace on its east side and the church of San Francesco di Paola on its west side.
text.directions_text: From Chiaia - Monte di Dio station (Metro Line 6), walk east for about 4 minutes. From Augusteo (Centrale funicular), walk south for about 6 minutes. From the Via Colombo - Porto stop (tram 1 and tram 4), walk south-west for about 13 minutes. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view down to the sea. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole colonnade and palace in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Vesuvius and the far end of the street closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m east of the subject, in Piazza del Plebiscito (the phone icon on the map), and face west. In the centre of the square, and face back toward the Royal Palace and the sea. From the centre you get a clear view down Via Cesario Console, with trees, the sea beyond and Vesuvius over the skyline. The edges of the square do not give the same clear line of sight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the middle of the street with the centre of the frame, so the trees lead the eye to the water. Keep the horizon level. For a second angle, shoot the curved colonnade toward the church from near the church side, or use the Royal Palace belvedere for a high view of the square (check the official site before you go).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or Vesuvius to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail. If people are walking through, the ultra-wide (0.5x) usually works better than panorama mode, because moving people can look distorted in a panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the square fills with visitors.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but it is sometimes used for events, so check the official site before you go.

The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) lets you fit the whole colonnade and palace in one frame.

name: Castel Sant'Elmo
label: Castel Sant'Elmo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (way/27182911): middle (276 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29403971: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castel Sant'Elmo' (295 m across).

text.description:
Castel Sant'Elmo is a medieval fortress on the Vomero hill above Naples, next to the Certosa di San Martino. This view of it is a distant, city-context shot taken from Piazza del Plebiscito in the historic centre. From the square the castle is a small, solid shape on the ridge, so it works best as part of a wider Naples scene rather than a close portrait.

The site has a long history. Documents mention a structure here from 1275, in the time of Charles of Anjou. The fortress took its present hexagonal star shape between 1537 and 1547, designed by the Valencian military architect Pedro Luis Escriva. It is built of volcanic tufa. It was a military prison until 1952, and today it is a museum, exhibition hall and office space.

From the square, give the castle room in the frame. Let the open space and the buildings below the hill fill the foreground, with the ridge and the fortress sitting above them. If you want the star-shaped walls and the bay, city and Vesuvius beyond the parapets, go up to the castle itself. Largo San Martino, beside the castle, is a quieter alternative with the Certosa di San Martino also in view. Entry details and opening days can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The castle stands on the Vomero hill above central Naples, next to the Certosa di San Martino. The photo is taken from Piazza del Plebiscito in the historic centre, looking up to the north-west.
text.directions_text: For the phone icon on the map, head for Piazza del Plebiscito in the historic centre and look to the north-west, up towards the Vomero ridge. To visit the castle itself, take the Centrale, Chiaia or Montesanto funicular to Corso Vittorio Emanuele, which is about 4 minutes on foot from the castle. Or take the Montesanto funicular to Morghen, also about 4 minutes on foot away. The phone icon on the map is about 1.1 km south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (3x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick the castle out on the ridge. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider shot with the square and the hill together. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the castle too small to read.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.1 km south-east of the subject, in Piazza del Plebiscito (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. From there the castle sits on the Vomero ridge to the north-west, seen at a distance over the city. This is a view of the fortress in its setting, not a close shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the ridge on the upper line, with the square and the city below it. Take one wide shot at the default lens (1x) for context and one zoomed shot for the castle. For the star-shaped walls close up, Castel Sant'Elmo itself is the better place, and Largo San Martino beside it is a quieter alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady when zoomed, as telephoto shots blur easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a clear day, as haze can flatten the distant ridge. Morning or late afternoon light usually gives the hillside more shape than midday.

text.access_note: Piazza del Plebiscito is an open public square; the castle itself is a museum site whose opening days and ticket rules should be checked on the official site before you go.

name: Castel dell'Ovo
label: Castel dell'Ovo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Partenope' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via Partenope nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/338168783: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castle dell'Ovo' (239 m across).

text.description: Castel dell'Ovo, the "Egg Castle", sits on a small rocky peninsula that was once the island of Megaride, with the Gulf of Naples all around it. It is the oldest castle in Naples. The name comes from an old legend that the poet Virgil hid a magic egg in its foundations, and that the castle would fall if the egg ever broke. The Normans built the first castle here in the 12th century, and its present form dates mostly from the Aragonese period in the 15th century. The long, low shape of about 200 by 45 metres, and the causeway of a little over 100 metres leading to it, make it easy to fit into a phone frame. The classic view is from the Via Partenope lungomare, on the stretch west of the castle between Mergellina and the castle, looking east. From there the castle sits on its promontory with Vesuvius rising behind it across the bay. The castle faces south-southwest, so afternoon and late afternoon light is kinder, while mornings tend to be backlit. For a second picture, walk down to Borgo Marinari, the little harbour beside the castle. Colourful fishing boats make a good foreground there, with the castle walls rising behind. Check the official site on the day if you want to go inside, as the castle may not always be open. Photographing it from the street and the harbour needs no ticket.
text.geographic_location: Castel dell'Ovo stands on the seafront between the San Ferdinando and Chiaia districts of Naples, on a small peninsula beside the Borgo Marinari harbour. It faces Mergellina across the water.
text.directions_text: From Chiaia - Monte di Dio station (Metro Line 6), the castle is about 900 m away in a straight line, to the south, so head south towards the sea. From Augusteo (Centrale funicular) it is about 1.2 km, also to the south. Once you reach the waterfront, the castle is the long building on the promontory. The phone icon on the map is about 150 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the castle and bay together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want the whole seafront in the frame, and try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Vesuvius closer behind the castle when you shoot the classic view from the Via Partenope lungomare, looking east.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 150 m north of the subject, on Via Partenope (the phone icon on the map), and face south. For the classic postcard angle with Vesuvius rising behind the castle over the bay, walk to the Via Partenope lungomare west of the castle and look east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the castle on one of the lower lines, with the sea in front and sky above. Keep the horizon level. From the lungomare west of the castle, looking east, Vesuvius can sit above and behind it. For a different picture, go to Borgo Marinari and shoot the colourful wooden boats in the foreground with the castle walls behind them. The Terrace of the Cannons is another option, with the cannons in the foreground and a wide view over the bay; use panorama mode there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and Vesuvius keep their colour. If you are shooting towards the light, check the screen and take a second shot with a different exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon or late afternoon, when the light falls on the castle's face. Mornings are backlit.

text.access_note: The seafront and harbour are open public space, but whether you can go inside the castle may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Castel Nuovo (Maschio Angioino)
label: Castel Nuovo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Municipio' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Municipio' (relation/7778893): middle (390 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15009683: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castel Nuovo' (182 m across).

text.description: Castel Nuovo, also called the Maschio Angioino, is a medieval castle that looks out over Piazza del Municipio in central Naples. Building began in 1279, and it served as a royal seat for kings of Naples, Aragon and Spain until 1815. The look you see today comes from the Aragonese rebuilding under Alfonso V, which began in 1453 and was finished in 1479. That rebuilding gave the castle its five round towers in Catalan Gothic style. It also added the white marble Triumphal Arch between the towers, the best-known detail of the building. The castle photographs well because the dark, heavy towers stand out against the open square and the sky, and the pale arch gives a clear point of interest in the middle. From the square you can fit the whole front into one frame, which suits a phone well. Stand back far enough to include the towers, keep the phone level so the walls do not lean, and use the gridlines to line up the arch with the centre of the picture. For a second picture, walk closer and use the zoom to isolate the arch between the two towers. The square is used for events, and the ramparts beside it host concerts in summer and an ice rink in winter, so temporary structures may appear in your frame.
text.geographic_location: Castel Nuovo stands in the centre of Naples, beside Piazza del Municipio and close to the city hall (Palazzo San Giacomo), near the port.
text.directions_text: Take Metro Line 1 or Metro Line 6 to Municipio station. The castle is to the south of the station, about 2 minutes on foot. The nearest tram stops are Via Colombo - Porto (about 250 m away) and Molo Piccolo (about 470 m away), served by tram 1 and tram 4; the castle is to the south-west of both stops. From the phone icon on the map, the castle is to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the full castle front with the square and the port behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the towers will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the marble arch between the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m north of the subject, in Piazza del Municipio (the phone icon on the map), and face south. From here the whole castle front is in view, with its round towers framed by the open square and the harbour and port activity behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the phone upright and level, and use the gridlines to keep the towers straight. Leave some open square and sky in the frame so the castle looks as large as it is. For an alternative, go closer to the castle itself and frame the white marble Triumphal Arch between the two dark towers, using the telephoto or a few steps back to avoid distortion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white marble arch to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky stays blue. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 8:30, when one blog suggests the sky behind the towers is clear. A tip says to stand near the palm trees. Summer afternoons can be hot, with harsh light.

text.access_note: You can photograph the castle's exterior from the public square; the museum inside is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.

Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep detail in pale marble (general phone advice).

name: Royal Palace of Naples
label: Royal Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Plebiscito' (way/27182911): middle (276 m across).

text.description: The Royal Palace of Naples fills one whole side of Piazza del Plebiscito, and that is what makes it so easy to photograph: the long main façade, with its row of ruler statues, sits behind a big open square that gives you room to step back. Work began in 1600 under the architect Domenico Fontana, for the Spanish viceroys. From 1734 the Bourbons made it their main home, and after a fire in 1837 the palace was almost completely rebuilt. Today the western half is a museum of the Royal Apartment and the eastern half is home to the National Library. The phone icon on the map is in the centre of the square, facing the main façade. From there the palace lies to the east, and Mount Vesuvius is sometimes visible behind it. Some guides suggest centring the frame for symmetry, so line up the middle of the building with the middle of your screen and keep the phone level. Once you have the full façade, walk a little closer for a second shot of the statues. The palace interior is a separate, ticketed visit, so this spot is about the outside view.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Naples, on the west side of the city centre near the port. The palace stands on Piazza del Plebiscito, close to Piazza del Municipio and the Teatro di San Carlo.
text.directions_text: From Municipio (Metro Line 1 or Metro Line 6), the palace is about 380 m on foot to the south-west. From Augusteo (Centrale funicular) it is about 370 m on foot, to the south-east. Once you reach the palace, the phone icon on the map is a short walk out into the middle of Piazza del Plebiscito, facing the main façade. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole long façade and the open square in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the centre of the building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m west of the subject, in Piazza del Plebiscito (the phone icon on the map), and face east. In the centre of the square, facing the palace's main façade. This view shows the long façade with its row of ruler statues, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the middle of the façade on the central vertical line for a symmetrical postcard shot. Keep the phone level so the horizontal lines of the building stay straight. Leave a little sky above the roofline, where Vesuvius may appear behind. Then step closer and zoom in on the statues for a second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is calm and mostly empty. Late afternoon or sunset light on the façade is also recommended by some guides.

text.access_note: The square is outdoors, but the palace interior is a separate visit and parts of the palace and gardens may be closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Quartieri Spagnoli and the Maradona mural
label: Quartieri Spagnoli
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo Maradona' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Largo Maradona' (way/1074336627): middle (3 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5294455978: the OpenStreetMap point 'Quartieri Spagnoli'.

text.description:
The Quartieri Spagnoli is a tight grid of steep, narrow streets just off Via Toledo, and its best-known photo is the Maradona mural on Via Emanuele de Deo. The painting rises several storeys up the side of a building. At street level below it is a little shrine of candles, scarves and football shirts, so you get a huge portrait and a close-up of everyday devotion in the same view. The streets around it give you washing lines, steep stairways and ground-floor homes that open straight onto the lane.

The quarter dates from the 16th century, when it was laid out to house Spanish soldiers. It has a grid of about eighteen streets by twelve and around 14,000 residents. Tourism grew sharply after Toledo Metro station opened beside it in 2012.

For photos, Largo Maradona is the classic spot. This widened stretch of the street faces the mural from the foot of the building, and it is free to see at any hour. It gets very crowded, so be patient and keep hold of your phone, as there are pickpocket warnings. Step back for the whole wall, then move close for the shrine. The mural's face can be hidden by an open bathroom window in the flat behind it, so check when you arrive. A redevelopment of the square was reported as approved for 2026, so parts of it may be under works. For a quieter alternative, the lane Vico Giardinetto is reported to have a 'la Mano de Dios' mural.
text.geographic_location: In the Quartieri Spagnoli, the grid of streets in central Naples just beside Via Toledo and Toledo Metro station. The mural is on Via Emanuele de Deo, at Largo Maradona.
text.directions_text: Take Metro Line 1 to Toledo station. The quarter lies to the south-west of the station, and it is about 4 minutes on foot to the mural area. Alternatively, the Centrale funicular stops at Augusteo, where the area lies to the north, about 5 minutes on foot. Look for Via Emanuele de Deo and the crowd gathered at Largo Maradona. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole mural and the shrine in a narrow street. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the candles, scarves and shirts.

text.description: Piazza Bellini is a lively square in Naples' historic centre, with a statue of Bellini, bars around its edges, and the remains of an ancient Greek city wall set into the ground. The excavated wall blocks sit on the western side of the square, against the older buildings, and a fence encloses them, so you shoot from outside it. The viewpoint along Via Santa Maria di Costantinopoli gives a different angle: a side-on look along the western edge, where the wall remains meet the buildings. Nearby, the Complesso di Sant'Antonio delle Monache a Port'Alba has an elegant staircase up to an eighteenth-century convent facade, with the square opening out below. It makes a good second shot if you have time. The square is very busy on evenings with people from the bars, so expect people in your frame after dark. If you want a clearer view of the stones, come when it is quieter. Keep your phone at a steady height and look for straight lines in the wall and the building edges.

text.description:
Naples Cathedral, also called the Cathedral of the Assumption of Mary or the Cathedral of Saint Januarius, is the main church of Naples and the seat of its archbishop. The present building is Angevin Gothic. It was commissioned by Charles I of Anjou and finished in the early 14th century under Robert of Anjou. It stands on the foundations of two early Christian basilicas. The façade was reworked in the late 19th century by Enrico Alvino, but it keeps its 15th-century portal. The cathedral also holds a vial of the blood of Saint Januarius, the city's patron saint, which is brought out three times a year.

For a photo, the challenge is that the cathedral is squeezed between older buildings, so a neat full-length shot from the ground is hard. The phone icon on the map is on Via Duomo, where the pedestrianised stretch in front lets you stand and look toward the building. From there the cathedral sits at the end of the street between historic palazzi, which shows how it fits into the old city. A short step back along the street gives you more room. If you want the façade to fill the frame, the nearby Piazzetta della Guglia del Duomo is a good alternative, with its porticoed square in the foreground. The façade may sometimes be covered by a temporary installation, so don't be surprised if it looks different from older pictures.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the old city of Naples, beside the Archbishop's Palace and the early Christian church of Santa Restituta.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Duomo on Metro Line 1, about 580 m from the cathedral, which lies to the north from there. Museo station, also on Metro Line 1, is about 690 m from the cathedral, which lies to the east from there. From the phone icon on the map, the cathedral is a short way to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the street is narrow and the cathedral is hemmed in by buildings. The default lens (1x) works well once you have stepped back, and the telephoto (2x or more) is good for the portal and façade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, on Via Duomo (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. On the pedestrianised stretch in front of the cathedral, and look to the north-east toward the building. From here the cathedral is framed at the end of the street between historic palazzi.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the street centred, so the palazzi on each side lead the eye to the cathedral. Hold the phone level to stop the buildings leaning inwards. If you want a tighter, façade-filling shot instead, try Piazzetta della Guglia del Duomo, where the porticoed square makes a natural foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a wide shot and a zoomed detail shot for variety.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer on a narrow street, with fewer people in your frame. There is no set best time, so go whenever the street looks clear.

name: Lungomare and Via Caracciolo

text.description:
Via Caracciolo and the Lungomare make up the long waterfront promenade that curves along the Bay of Naples. Seen from the water's edge it is a ribbon of road and seafront. Seen from above, it becomes one sweeping curve with the hill of San Martino and Posillipo behind it. The best phone photo of it is therefore taken from the upper terrace and battlements of Castel dell'Ovo, looking back along Via Caracciolo toward Posillipo. From up there you look down onto the waterfront, with the hill and the open bay beyond.

Check on the day whether the castle is open before you rely on this view. If you can't get up, Via Francesco Caracciolo itself is a good alternative. From there the bay curves round with Castel dell'Ovo on the left and Vesuvius in the distance. Borgo Marinaro is another option, with the castle towers and rocks in the foreground and the waterfront receding toward Posillipo. On clear days you may see the Amalfi direction in the distance.

Some viewpoints along Via Caracciolo may be blocked by construction, so be ready to shift along the promenade for a clear line of sight. The road may also be car-free mainly on Sunday mornings. Treat that as a possibility rather than a rule.
text.geographic_location: The promenade runs along the seafront of Naples, between the Chiaia waterfront by Castel dell'Ovo and the Mergellina end toward Posillipo.
text.directions_text: Start at S. Antonio on the Mergellina funicular, where the promenade lies to the east, about 4 minutes on foot. San Gioacchino, also on the Mergellina funicular, is another place to begin. The phone icon on the map is about 2.3 km east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the terrace to fit the waterfront, the hill and the bay in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the curve of the road. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from Via Francesco Caracciolo to pull Vesuvius closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 2.3 km east of the subject, at Castel dell'Ovo (the phone icon on the map), and face west. The photo looks back over Via Caracciolo toward Posillipo. It shows a high view down onto the waterfront, the hill of San Martino and Posillipo, with the bay beyond. The stretch of promenade you are photographing lies to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the curve of the waterfront along one of the lower lines, with the hill and sky above it. Keep the horizon level. Use the battlements as a foreground edge if they suit your shot. If the castle is closed, try Via Francesco Caracciolo with the castle on the left and Vesuvius in the distance. Borgo Marinaro is a second alternative, with the castle towers and rocks in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the far hill to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. For the long view of Vesuvius, hold the phone steady against a wall or railing at 3x-5x. A Live Photo can also catch moving traffic or waves.

text.description: Gesù Nuovo is a church whose front looks more like a fortress than a place of worship. The whole facade is covered in rough, pointed stone blocks, like the facets of a cut diamond. That texture is why it photographs so well: it catches light and shadow and gives even a simple phone shot plenty of detail. The front was not designed for a church at all. It was built in 1470 for a palace belonging to Roberto Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno. The Jesuits bought the property in the 1580s and built the church behind the old front between 1584 and 1601, keeping the unusual stonework. The church stands on a square that grew up in the early 16th century, when Naples expanded westwards. In the middle of the square is the tall, ornate spire dedicated to the Immaculate Virgin. It makes a good foreground and shows you where you are. The Gothic church and convent of Santa Chiara is next door, so the square is a good place to linger. The best view is from the far side of the square, looking back at the facade with the spire in front. From there the whole building fits in one frame. For a detail shot, go close to the stone and photograph the engraved marks on the blocks. The square tends to be crowded around midday, so allow a moment for people to clear your frame.
text.geographic_location: Gesù Nuovo is on the square of the same name, just beyond the western edge of Naples' historic centre. It stands beside the Santa Chiara complex, a short walk from Dante metro station (Metro Line 1).
text.directions_text: From Dante (Metro Line 1), walk south-east and you reach the square after about 200 m on foot. From Università (Metro Line 1), head north-west, about 540 m on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and the spire. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you have to stand close. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stonework.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the spire. Keep the phone upright and level so the building doesn't lean. Put the spire in the lower foreground and the facade behind it. For a second picture, go close to the front and use telephoto to fill the frame with the rough stone blocks and the marks engraved on them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the facade doesn't wash out against the sky. For the stone close-up, hold the phone steady and let the surface fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The first hour after sunrise is best, or a lightly overcast day. Harsh midday sun flattens the stone texture, and the square is busiest around then. Morning or late afternoon also works.

text.description:
The Fontana del Gigante is a 17th-century fountain with three round arches, and it now stands on Via Partenope, close to Castel dell'Ovo. It was commissioned by the Spanish viceroy, the Duke of Alba, and designed by Pietro Bernini and Michelangelo Naccherino. The fountain takes its name from a colossal statue, the Giant, that once stood beside it near the Royal Palace. It has been moved several times, and reached its present spot in 1905-06. Look closely and you will see river gods holding sea monsters in the side arches, a cup held up by two sea creatures in the middle, and a pair of caryatids with cornucopias at the ends.

It photographs well because the white stonework stands against open water, with the Gulf of Naples behind it and Mount Vesuvius rising in the distance. The best frame is taken from the phone icon on the map, at the curve on the seafront side where the two streets meet. From there the fountain sits about 20 m to the south-east, with the bay and Vesuvius behind it. One blog suggests the view is best when you approach from Castel dell'Ovo. Go early or late in the day, when the light is softer and it is usually quieter. Visitors have reported roadworks nearby and the fountain being closed or dry at times, so the scene may differ from the photos.

text.directions_text: From Chiaia - Monte di Dio on Metro Line 6, head south-east towards the seafront and Via Partenope; it is about 775 m on foot. The Augusteo stop on the Centrale funicular is further away, about 1 km on foot, and the fountain lies to the south of it. You can also walk along the seafront from Castel dell'Ovo, which gives the approach one blog recommends. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Stand on Via Partenope, at the curve where the two streets meet on the seafront side of the fountain. The three white arches sit against the Gulf of Naples with Mount Vesuvius rising behind them.

Keep the phone level so the arches and horizon stay straight. For a different view, walk to the promenade side, where the bay and Vesuvius show beyond the fountain, or line the arches up to frame the open sea with Vesuvius in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright stonework and sky keep their detail. Take a few frames in case people or traffic wander into the shot.

name: Santa Chiara and its cloister
label: Santa Chiara
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Gesù Nuovo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Gesù Nuovo' (way/563345000): middle (121 m across).

text.description:
Santa Chiara is a large religious complex in the historic centre of Naples: a church, a monastery, royal tombs and a museum. It was built between 1313 and 1340 by Queen Sancha of Majorca and her husband King Robert of Naples, and Robert is buried here. The church is a plain, tall rectangle, about 110 m long inside the walls, with no apse. The bell tower stands apart from the main building, which makes it easy to pick out. Wartime bombing and fire damaged the church in 1943, and the restoration was completed in 1953.

From the square outside, the exterior is the part you can photograph freely. The long, simple walls and the separate bell tower fit well into a phone frame across the open space. Inside the complex, the majolica cloister is the colourful highlight. It has octagonal pillars covered in painted tiles, added in 1742 in a Rococo style, and they frame the garden and the sky.

For the exterior, stand back in the square and use the gridlines to keep the walls and tower upright. Use the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, or 2x to pick out the tower. The cloister is a paid entry and a place of worship sits next to it, so check the official site before you go. Then use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the cloister to take in the tiled pillars and benches.
text.geographic_location: Santa Chiara is in the historic centre of Naples, on Via Benedetto Croce, the easternmost stretch of Spaccanapoli. Its façade is diagonally across from the church of Gesù Nuovo and Piazza del Gesù Nuovo.
text.directions_text: From Dante (Metro Line 1), Santa Chiara is to the south-east, about 5 minutes on foot. From Università (Metro Line 1) it is to the north-west, about 7 minutes on foot. Head for Piazza del Gesù Nuovo, which is the phone icon on the map, and the church is just to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m west of the subject, in Piazza del Gesù Nuovo (the phone icon on the map), and face east. From here you see the church's exterior with its freestanding bell tower across the open square, and the church lies to the east.

Leave some open square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. If you go inside, the tiled pillars and benches of the majolica cloister (Chiostro maiolicato) make a good alternative, with the garden and sky framed between them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Inside the cloister, tap a brightly tiled pillar and adjust the exposure so the colours stay rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and a quieter square, but check the cloister's visiting hours first.

name: Fontanelle Cemetery

camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Fontanelle cemetery'.

text.description:
The Fontanelle Cemetery is an ossuary inside a cave in the tuff hillside of the Materdei district. It holds the bones of a great many Naples residents, most of them poor and unnamed. Many came from the plague of 1656, and more were added over the following centuries. In 1872 Father Gaetano Barbati had the remains disinterred and catalogued, and they were then kept above ground in makeshift crypts, boxes and racks. In the following decades local people took to caring for individual skulls, bringing flowers and giving them names. The church authorities closed the site in 1969, and it has since been restored and can be visited.

It photographs well because of the scale. Long, tall cavern spaces are lined with stacked bones and skulls, and the rock and the dim light give everything a strong mood. Your phone can work with that, but this is a place of remembrance, so keep your photos respectful. Avoid posed or joking pictures, and do not touch or move anything. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long cave perspectives and the default lens (1x) for more natural views. Zoom in for details such as a single shelf or a small offering. Photography rules and entry arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: The Certosa di San Martino is a former Carthusian monastery on the Vomero hill, high above the city, and it sits right beside Castel Sant'Elmo. The monks finished it in 1368 under Joan I of Naples. It was enlarged in the 1500s and again in 1623 under the architect Cosimo Fanzago, who gave it the baroque form you see today. It is now a museum, known for its Nativity scenes (presepe). The whole complex is about 220 m across, so it is large enough that you will want to choose what to photograph. The best phone picture here is the view from the terrace in front of the entrance, rather than the building itself. From the phone icon on the map you look out over the Gulf of Naples, with Vesuvius in the background and the city's rooftops stepping down below. On clear days Capri shows on the horizon. Because the terrace is open ground, it is easy to take several frames at different zoom levels without holding anyone up. If you also want a calmer, tree-framed view over the Vomero hillside, Villa Floridiana is another recommended viewpoint. Go early if you can, as the terrace tends to be emptier and the light softer.
text.geographic_location: In the Vomero district, on the hilltop above central Naples, next to Castel Sant'Elmo. The viewpoint is the terrace in front of the Certosa entrance, at Largo San Martino.
text.directions_text: Start at Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the stop for the Centrale, Chiaia and Montesanto funiculars. The Certosa is to the north-east, about 3 minutes on foot. You can also reach the Vomero by metro to Vanvitelli metro station and walk to the terrace from there. Once at the entrance, the phone icon on the map is on the Belvedere terrace in front of it. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view of the bay and Vesuvius. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long monastery frontage in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Vesuvius or the waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north of the subject, on Belvedere San Martino (the phone icon on the map), and face south. In front of the Certosa entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a top or bottom line so the bay stays level. Include a strip of rooftops in the foreground to give a sense of height. For the building, face south towards the monastery (about 112 m from where you stand), use ultra-wide and keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone upright. If you want a calmer alternative view, Villa Floridiana is another recommended viewpoint, with a tree-framed look over the hillside and city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on Vesuvius to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. For the full sweep of the bay, try panorama mode and pan slowly. Hazy days soften distant shapes, so a little zoom helps.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soon after the museum opens, when the light is softer and the terrace is emptier. One guide says the monastery façade is backlit in the afternoon, so the building shot is best earlier.

text.access_note: The Belvedere terrace in front of the entrance is an open public viewpoint, but the museum and the terrace inside the Certosa are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

Walk a few steps along the viewpoint before settling, because small changes in position can clear a lamp post or a tree from the view. Keep your phone close to your body when taking it in and out of your pocket, as any busy lookout can be crowded. text.description: Porta Capuana is a Renaissance city gate on the eastern edge of Naples' old centre. It was rebuilt and moved to this spot in 1484, when the city grew eastwards and new walls went up. Two bastions from the older walls still stand on either side. The walls around it were later taken down, so the gate now stands on its own and looks a bit like a triumphal arch. That is why it photographs so well: a clear, symmetrical front with a tower on each side, and plenty of carved detail in the stone. The carvings on the 1484 facings show classical-style trophies and flying Victories. Just inside the gate is the domed church of Santa Caterina a Formiello, which can add a second shape behind the arch if you step back far enough. Despite the name, this was not the ancient Roman road gate to Capua. It was a later rebuild, so don't go looking for Roman stonework. For the full front with both towers, use the phone icon on the map, in Piazza San Francesco a Capuana. If you have time, Piazza Enrico De Nicola, on the Castel Capuano side, gives a less usual view of the gate from behind. Traffic around the gate is heavy, so use the crossings and don't step into the road for a better angle. Conditions can change, and building work has sometimes hidden the gate, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: Porta Capuana is on the eastern side of Naples' historic centre, in the Porta Capuana district of the Fourth Municipality. It stands not far from Castel Capuano and close to the Garibaldi station area.
text.directions_text: From Garibaldi station (Metro Line 1, tram 1 and tram 2), walk north-west for about 400 m to reach the gate. If you come by tram, the Principe Umberto stop (tram 1 and tram 2) is about 200 m east of the gate. From there, head for Piazza San Francesco a Capuana, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole gate and both towers. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if parked vehicles or traffic force you to stand close. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carved panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m east of the subject, in Piazza San Francesco a Capuana (the phone icon on the map), and face west. On the side of the square facing the gate. From here the full front is in view, with both surviving towers and the Renaissance carvings framed by the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central arch up with the middle vertical line, so the towers sit evenly either side. Keep your phone level so the towers don't lean. Include a little of the square in the foreground to show the gate's scale. For something different, Piazza Enrico De Nicola on the Castel Capuano side shows the gate from behind, but treat that as the second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the carvings keep their detail. Take a few shots in a row, as moving traffic can get into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the stone. The stonework can glow just before sunset.

text.description: Toledo is a Metro Line 1 station on Via Toledo, and it is a good place for photos even if you only came to catch a train. It opened in 2012 and was designed by the Spanish architect Óscar Tusquets. Water is the main theme. Building the station meant dealing with an underground aquifer, and the design plays on that. On the way down, the ochre tiling recalls Neapolitan tuff stone. It then gives way to Robert Wilson's Sea Gallery, a space covered entirely in mosaic with wave-like lighting and a pillar shaped like a fountain jet. One large mosaic by William Kentridge, on the mezzanine, shows Neapolitan life with nods to Pompeii and Vesuvius. A second one, met on the way down, shows a cart with symbols of the 1799 Parthenopean Republic. Pieces of the old Aragonese walls found during the digging are also on show. At street level on Via Diaz, three hexagonal skylights clad in blue and ochre tiles hint at the colours below. Nearby stands Kentridge's rusty-steel horseman, Il Cavaliere di Toledo. The station won an international public-building award in 2013 and a tunnelling award in 2015, and the Daily Telegraph named it the most beautiful in Europe. For photos, look for strong lines: the escalators, the curves of the Sea Gallery and the blue tiles. Keep clear of other passengers and of the barriers while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Toledo station sits directly on Via Toledo in central Naples, with exits towards Piazza Carità and Piazza del Plebiscito, on Via Diaz and at Piazza Montecalvario. Via Diaz has been pedestrianised in front of it.
text.directions_text: If you are travelling by Metro, take Line 1 to Toledo station. From Augusteo (Centrale funicular) it is about 7 minutes on foot, heading north. From the tram 1 and tram 4 stop at Via Colombo - Porto, walk north-west for about 10 minutes. From Molo Piccolo (also tram 1 and tram 4) walk west for about 11 minutes. shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and use the escalator handrails and the curved mosaic walls as leading lines. In the Sea Gallery, keep the camera level so the curves look smooth. Let a passing figure walk through the frame to give a sense of scale, or wait for a clear moment if you want an empty shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-bright part of the wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lit areas keep their colour. Hold the phone against a wall or rail, with both hands, to keep it steady, and use night mode only if the picture looks dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning or mid-morning on a weekday tends to be quieter inside. Come in daylight if you want the outdoor skylights on Via Diaz.
